findings.issue: Source “As one who has grown a fine young olive tree…” is rendered “A man grows a fine young olive tree in a clear place”, which reads as a bare statement and drops the simile marker; the comparison is only recoverable later.
findings.fix: As he spoke he struck Menelaus squarely on the shield, but the spear did not go through, because the shield bent its point back. Then Menelaus took aim and prayed to father Zeus. Euphorbus was drawing back, and Menelaus struck him at the base of the throat, leaning his whole weight on the spear to drive it home. The point went straight through his neck. He fell heavily to the ground, and his armor clattered around him. His hair, which was like the hair of the Graces, and his locks so neatly bound in bands of silver and gold, were all soaked with blood. Think of a man who has grown a fine young olive tree in a clear place with plenty of water. The plant is full of promise, and though the winds beat on it from every direction, it keeps putting out its white blossoms, until the blasts of some fierce hurricane sweep down and level it with the ground. In the same way Menelaus stripped the fair youth Euphorbus of his armor after he had killed him. Or think of a fierce lion on the mountains, proud of his strength, who fastens on the finest heifer in a herd as it feeds. First he breaks her neck with his strong jaws, and then he gorges on her blood and entrails. Dogs and shepherds raise a hue and cry against him, but they keep their distance and will not come close, for they are pale with fear. In the same way no one had the courage to face valiant Menelaus. The son of Atreus would then have carried off the armor of the son of Panthous with ease, if Phoebus Apollo had not been angry. In the form of Mentes, chief of the Cicons, Apollo urged Hector to attack him. “Hector,” he said, “you are chasing after the horses of the noble son of Aeacus, but you will not take them. A mortal man cannot hold them in hand and drive them, except Achilles, whose mother is immortal. Meanwhile Menelaus son of Atreus has stood over the body of Patroclus and killed the noblest of the Trojans, Euphorbus son of Panthous, so that he can fight no more.”

findings.issue: Source “As when Jove bends his bright bow in heaven in token to mankind… even so… did Minerva”; candidate “Zeus bends his bright bow in heaven as a sign to mankind” is stated as a plain fact with no comparison marker, so the simile half reads as narration.
findings.fix: Now the fierce, groaning fight raged again around Patroclus, because Athena had come down from heaven and stirred up its fury. Far-seeing Zeus, who had changed his mind, had commanded her and sent her to encourage the Danaans. Just as Zeus bends his bright bow in heaven as a sign to mankind of either war or the chill storms that keep men from their work and plague their flocks, in the same way, wrapped in such radiant raiment, Athena went into the host and spoke to each man in turn. First she took the form and voice of Phoenix and spoke to Menelaus son of Atreus, who was standing near her. “Menelaus,” she said, “it will be a shame and a dishonor to you if dogs tear apart the noble comrade of Achilles under the walls of Troy. So stand firm, and urge your men to do the same.”

findings.issue: Source “He knew that he was not to sack the city neither with nor without himself” has an ambiguous “he”; candidate resolves it to Patroclus (“Patroclus was not going to sack the city, with him or without him”). Plausible reading, but the pronoun is resolved to a named person.
Butler’s “I doubt that we shall not stay Hector” is garbled; candidate “I doubt that we can hold back Hector” takes a sensible reading.
Butler’s “at the loo of a band of young huntsmen” is a garbled/typo phrase; candidate “running at the head of a band of young huntsmen” is an interpretation not stated in the source.
